body: Halftime. The big screen says SAINTS 28 · LIONS 10 in numbers taller than Kevin, and all of Sully’s sits down at once and orders more fries. The owner has rung the bell four times and is rolling his shoulder like a relief pitcher. On the corner TV Adrian Peterson goes through the middle of the Browns again, untouched, and Jack puts his head back against the booth and asks God, out loud and with real feeling, what exactly Cleveland ever did to Him. The Steelers table applauds.

Laney is redoing her face for the second half. Out of a gold clutch the size of a sandwich come a compact, a lip gloss and a gold eyeliner pencil, which she uncaps and aims at her own eyelid. Lena reaches across Kevin and takes it out of her hand. “Sugar. That is a thirty-dollar pencil.” “Then it’s going to a good cause.” And Lena turns on the booth seat, one knee up on the red vinyl, to face Jack.

“Hold still, Youngstown.” She puts her left hand flat along his jaw to keep his face where she wants it, her fingers still cool from her glass, and sets the pencil on his left cheekbone just under the place where the scar runs out of his eyebrow. It’s cold, and then it isn’t. She works close. Her thumb rests at the corner of his mouth for exactly as long as the job needs it there. She frowns at his face the way she frowns at a Greek participle, and her breath smells of Coke and lime. A stem. A band across it. The curl of one petal, out and down.

Her LG goes off on the table beside the Coke and keeps going, buzz after buzz, walking itself toward the edge. She flips it open with her free hand without taking the other off his jaw, and because his face is exactly where she’s put it, the screen is right under his eyes.

body.text: WHO DATTT BREES IS GOD LUC SAYS HEYY

body: Another lands under it before she can close it, all capitals, missing the same letters. Somewhere behind them is the Superdome at half past one, seventy thousand people in black and gold, Luc, and the boy she’s been with since she was sixteen, a phone in his fist. Something comes up into her face, quick and bright, and goes. “He’s spelling like Laney,” she says. Laney, who has an opinion about everything, lets that one go by. Lena shuts the phone with her thumb and lays it face down by her glass.

Then she’s back on his face, and finds him looking at her, and her eyes come up off the pencil to meet his from four inches away. “I’m not fine, Costigan,” she says. “I’m *ecstatic*. Note the difference.”

Nobody at the table says a word about any of it. Margot is studying the halftime show with professional interest. Kevin is reading the fries. Theo has his chin on his fist and an expression of total serenity, which is how Jack knows he will be hearing about this until Easter. Laney’s pink BlackBerry comes up over the top of a menu and says it for all of them: a soft fake shutter, no flash.

Lena goes back to the petal. Jack keeps still, and keeping still turns out to be harder physical work than anything the Hobart has asked of him at one in the morning: her palm along his jaw, her thumb at the corner of his mouth, the pencil going round in small cold strokes, her lips parted in concentration a hand’s width from his, and every muscle he owns asking leave to turn his face one inch into her hand, and every one of them told no. Her eyes are on her work. Then, for the space of a breath, they aren’t.

response: He holds through the second petal and the third, and through one more stroke on the left one that it didn’t need. She knows it didn’t, and does it anyway. Then she sits back with her head on one side and considers what she’s made. “There,” she says. “Now you’re ours.” She’s turned back to the screen before the teams are even out of the tunnel, the pencil crosswise in her teeth, and his cheekbone is cold where the gold is and warm everywhere else.

Her mouth goes flat with the effort of not rewarding that. “That’s Matthew five,” she says, “and no.” She caps the pencil on the *no* with a click, presses the last curl in with the pad of her thumb, and hands the pencil back across the table to Laney without looking at either of them. The fleur-de-lis is finished whether he likes it or not. He likes it.

She tells him while she finishes it, not looking up. Louis, the saint and the king, and the lilies on the old French flags. Joan of Arc in gold leaf on her horse on Decatur Street. The city flag. The helmets. And after the storm, on every blue-tarp roof and every FEMA trailer parked in front of a house with the waterline still on it: painted on plywood, stuck on bumpers, sprayed on the boards by people who came home to see what was left. She sets the last curl and blows on it once, a cool breath across his cheekbone. “It means home, Costigan,” she says. “It means we came back.”

body: He closes the laptop. On the far bed Theo looks up from the MacBook, studies Jack’s face for a while with something like tenderness, and wishes him a very holy Mass.

The nine o’clock is the college Mass, and the college has come to it: standing room under the overturned hull of the ceiling, kids on the side-aisle steps with their knees up, the overheads off and the candles lit, so the blue glass has gone black and the driftwood Christ hangs over the altar in a light that won’t keep still. Three guitars and a cajón. Kenzie Rourke cantors the psalm in a trained soprano that makes the freshmen look up — *I will walk before the Lord, in the land of the living* — and Peter Haddad reads Isaiah from the ambo like a man rehearsing for C-SPAN. *I gave my back to those who beat me, my cheeks to those who plucked my beard; my face I did not shield from buffets and spitting.* Then James: faith without works is dead. Then Mark, and the road to Caesarea Philippi. *But who do you say that I am?*

Lena is two rows up on the aisle in the black mantilla. From where Jack stands at the end of his pew he can see the scalloped edge of the lace and, under it at the nape of her neck, the thin gold chain.

Osei preaches from the step, reading glasses hanging on their cord, and doesn’t take long. “Peter gets the answer right,” he says. “Four verses later, Jesus calls him Satan.” He lets the four verses go by in the quiet. “Same man. Same afternoon. He did not trade him in.” He takes the glasses off. “So bring whichever Peter you brought tonight; that is the one He asked for.” And he sits, and two hundred college students who came braced for twenty minutes are left holding the rest of their attention.

At the sign of peace Lena turns to give it behind her — her hand to a girl in a Sigma Rho sweatshirt, her hand to the boy beside the girl — and her eyes go on past them, back two rows, and find Jack. Then they drop to his left cheekbone, and stop. Her mouth goes in hard at both corners. “Peace be with you,” she tells the Sigma Rho girl with enormous dignity, and faces front.

Through the Lamb of God her shoulders go. She gets the edge of the mantilla up against her mouth and holds it there, *have mercy on us*, and her shoulders keep going, *have mercy on us*, and the boy beside her looks over in real concern, and she nods to him over the lace that she is absolutely fine, *grant us peace*. Jack kneels with everybody else and has no idea what’s wrong with her, and is a little hurt.

Afterward the courtyard empties into the dark of the Grove in twos and threes. The broken sprinkler by the olive tree hisses away in the dark, still broken. Lena is waiting under the olive with the mantilla folded over her arm. Without a word she touches her own cheekbone. Jack puts his hand up to his face, and his fingertips come away gold.

“You received the Body of Christ,” she says, “in my fleur-de-lis.” “All day?” “Since halftime, Costigan. Through Sully’s, the parking lot, Kevin’s mother’s van and the Eucharist.” He thinks about the far bed in 412, and the very holy Mass. “Theo watched me walk out the door with it.” “Your roommate,” Lena says, “is a serpent, and I respect him.”

Mrs. Fitch comes across the flagstones in her lavender cardigan with a pink slip held out in front of her: WHILE YOU WERE OUT. “Mr. Costigan. Good. Your grandmother telephoned the rectory this afternoon. From Ohio.” She reads it off the slip, every word, in the voice of a woman reading the minutes. “*Mrs. Carmela Rinaldi, Youngstown. One Mass in thanksgiving for my grandson’s good confession. Ten dollars to follow by mail.*” She looks at him over it. “She asked me to underline *good*. I have underlined it. She also wished to know whether you are eating.”

Osei is coming past toward the rectory with his stole over his arm, the limp a little longer at the end of a Sunday. Mrs. Fitch hands him the slip for the Mass book. He reads it. He looks at Jack over the top of it, perfectly grave. “I can neither confirm nor deny that you have ever been in my confessional, Jack. Your grandmother can confirm it to the state of Ohio.” He folds the slip into his shirt pocket and goes on, and from the dark by the rectory door comes his laugh, once, from the belly, not hidden at all.

Lena has heard every word of it. She stands under the olive tree with the mantilla over her arm, looking at him, and it isn’t the red-pen look or the across-the-oak look. It’s a newer one, and he’d like to see it again.

response: “Then God bless Nonna,” Lena says. Plain, no theater, every syllable meant.

She settles the mantilla over her arm. “What did you yell at Him about at halftime?” “The Browns.” “Nobody yells at an empty room, Costigan.” His own line from Ocean Road, handed back as if she’d been keeping it somewhere safe. “Goodnight, Jack.” Then it’s the olive tree and Jack under the courtyard light, scrubbing at his cheekbone with a licked thumb and getting none of the gold off his face.

body: On Wednesday the marine layer sits on Hollis all day, and the sea window in 302 is a white sheet with a foghorn somewhere behind it. Yusuf has his head down on his arms, four days from Eid and conserving. Caleb has his *Consolations* out, more Post-it than book now, and under it, badly hidden, a brand-new hardback of *The Lost Symbol*, out yesterday. He sees Jack see it. “For research,” Caleb says.

body.text: Lena is already in her chair. She slides her two pages across the oak without looking up and holds out her hand, palm up, for his. “Mr. Costigan.” He puts his paper in it. It goes into the OCTAVIA tote, and she opens the Williams and is gone into it.
body.else: Lena is already in her chair, sleeves pushed to the elbow, which before one in the afternoon is a declaration of intent. “Give,” she says, and takes his two pages out of his hand before he’s sat down, and slides hers across the oak in the same motion.

body.title: PHIL 9H · Costigan
body.text:
That the Lucky Man Owes Nothing

A debt is a relation between two persons, and luck is not a person. Whatever the lucky man has, he borrowed from no one; and what was never lent cannot be owed.

body.title: PHIL 9H · Broussard
body.text:
That There Is Such a Thing as Luck

Providence does not abolish chance; it makes room for it. Aquinas says it would be contrary to providence if nothing in the world happened by chance (*SCG* III.74), because a world without accidents would be a world without secondary causes — no wind, no weather, no free men — and God did not make a clock.

body: At 1:07 Hale comes in with the wine on his cuff and doesn’t sit. “Williams’s Gauguin,” he says. “Abandons a wife and five children for Tahiti and paints masterpieces. Williams says he is justified, if he is justified at all, only by succeeding — and he can’t know whether he will succeed until he’s already gone. Had the paintings been bad, he’d merely be a cad with a steamer ticket. Discuss. Mr. Hargrove, I see you’re already vibrating.”

Lena gets there first anyway. “He left a wife and five children, Professor, and gave Tahiti syphilis.” Caleb comes in for Gauguin fast and a little flushed — the work outlasts the man, the man was never the point, some things are bigger than a family — and keeps going a while after the argument has stopped needing him. Yusuf lifts his head off his arms long enough to say that right now he would leave his family for a sandwich, and puts it back down.

Jack reads her paper under the edge of the oak while Caleb defends the steamer ticket. It’s very good. By the bottom of page two the providence girl has proved there’s such a thing as luck, cleanly, with Aquinas holding the door for her, and he goes back over it twice looking for the seam and can’t find one. He uncaps the red pen.
At the end of the hour the papers come back across the table, bled on.

body.text: His page one has one word on it in her red, top margin, dead center: *“Noted.”* Nothing else on either page. Not a circle, not a NO, not a single *cite me*. He turns the page over to be sure.
body.else: On his page one, top margin, in her red: *“You don’t believe a word of this. It’s your best paper.”* Underneath, smaller, an arrow to his first sentence and the word *coward*, which in her red ink is affectionate, he’s almost sure.

body: His own red is at the bottom of her page two, written in the last minute of the hour: *You proved it. I don’t think you were trying to.* She reads it standing, tote on her shoulder, while the San Diego boys file out around her. Then she reads it again.
Out on the Hollis steps, in the fog, the RAZR goes twice.

body: At 5:20 the RAZR goes off in his pocket. He tips the cracked screen until it lights: a number he doesn’t have saved, long, out of state, and he knows it anyway. He opens it. Across the road the speakers drop out between songs, and into the gap the recorded woman comes flat and loud enough for the whole bench: “This is a prepaid call from — Danny — an inmate at Trumbull Correctional Institution.” The name in the middle is in his brother’s own voice, hurried, dropped into the space she leaves for it.

Lena hears every word. She doesn’t look away, and she doesn’t look at him. She looks across Seacliff at the porch, at the girls in white and the girls in pink straw hats, and her hand goes up to the medal and holds it.

body.text: Monday stops here. Whatever it was, it doesn’t reach as far as a man taking a call from a prison: she stays exactly where she is, a foot away, keeping the bench with him.

s13c.slug: THURSDAY · 5:21 PM · THE BLUFF BENCH, SEACLIFF ROAD
body: He presses the key and stays where he is.

“*Professor.*” His brother, a little out of breath, a room full of men behind him and a steel door somewhere that buzzes and slams. The earpiece is loud enough that Lena could hear it if she wanted to, and she is looking very carefully at the porch. “Got your letter. *Sixty-six degrees. Green on top and gray underneath.*” Danny says it like he has it by heart, which he does. “I read it to Reggie in the next bunk. Reggie’s from Portsmouth. Never seen nothing bigger than the Ohio River. He wants to know does it smell.” “Like kelp.” “I don’t know what that is, Professor, and neither does Reggie.”

A pause with a television in it. “Hey. You never write when there’s nothing to say.” Another. “Somebody tell you to?” Jack looks at the water. “A guy at work.” “Tell him thanks.” Then, lighter, the old Danny coming back up into his voice: “Book’s in the mailroom. *Brideshead.* They read it before I do. Some C.O. has got it on his lunch break right now, finding out how it ends.”

Across the road the porch hits the chorus and sixty women scream the *oh-oh-oh* at the sky, and Danny stops. “Where are you, a zoo?” “Sorority thing.” A silence, and then, enormously scandalized and enormously pleased: “*Professor.*”

When he stands, she lifts a hand from her lap — go, ride safe — and stays where she is, watching the porch.

s14.slug: FRIDAY · 2:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The Thursday shift lets him go at twenty past one. Tonight Gloria rated a long-haul trucker to his face, *lemon meringue — all air*, and the trucker tipped her five dollars for it. At midnight Rudy put a plate of eggs on the steel by the Hobart and pointed at it with the spatula until the dish man ate. The RAZR charger came out from behind the machine furred with lint and smelling of bleach, and it’s coiled in his back pocket now beside the O’Connor. La Flaca got him up Mission and out Ocean Road in the cold, her coaster brakes complaining at every grade.

Delgado at ten past two. Through the lobby glass Marcus is asleep at the front desk again, organic chemistry this week, rising and falling on his chest. Jack sits down on the front steps instead of going in. The gold went down the drain on Tuesday — the last fleck of it came out of his eyebrow in the fourth-floor shower — and his face is just his face.
*Do you think the lucky one sleeps, Mr. Costigan?* He’s had four nights to come up with a better answer than the one he gave in Hollis 302. He’s still working on it.

At 2:10 the horn comes up off the bluff. Two long, one short, one long: the long notes low and patient, the short one a hitch in the middle, the last held out over the water until the fog takes the end of it. Then the freight itself, steel on steel down in the dark below the Lagoon, and the concrete step under him taking a share of the weight. Jack counts under his breath, the way he has since he was six, one car into the next, alone this time. The twenties. The forties. The sound goes on up the coast and thins and is gone.
Sixty.
At 2:14 the RAZR goes in his pocket.

body.text: Sixty-one. No second engine tonight. Goodnight, Jack. —L.

body: He reads it twice. Then he leans back on his elbows and looks up the face of the building. Every window on the second floor is dark, and one of them is open.

response: Nothing comes back. Nothing needs to. He sits with the phone open in his hand till the screen gives up its light on its own.

choices.text: Close the phone. Listen to the end of it.
response: He folds the RAZR shut and listens. The last of the freight is a long way north by now, more a pressure in the air than a sound, and then not even that; then just the surf down under the bluff, and the quiet coming back up it behind the train, one street at a time, until it reaches the steps.

s14b.slug: FRIDAY · 2:16 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He goes in. Marcus doesn’t wake; organic chemistry goes up and down. The elevator takes its time getting to four. The lounge is dark, the whiteboard a pale square on the far wall, and under the door of 412 there’s no light at all, Theo’s screen off, Theo a long shape under the comforter. Jack doesn’t turn on the lamp. He sets the O’Connor on the desk beside the Hopkins, squared up for October, and lays the RAZR next to them, open to her text, and lies down on top of the blanket in his clothes. The screen keeps her lit for the fifteen seconds it’s allowed — *Goodnight, Jack. —L.* — and then it goes dark, and he lies there with his eyes open, listening to the building breathe.
